events.excerpt: arXiv:2606.18651v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multiple Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) campaigns may execute concurrently, producing audit logs whose events are interleaved without explicit campaign boundaries. We formulate this setting as Unknown-K Interleaved Sequence Demixing (UKISD): recovering coherent campaign episodes when the number of concurrent campaigns is unknown. Each episode is represented as a sequence of MITRE ATT&CK technique occurrences, and demixing is cast as occurrence-level assignment with sequence reconstruction. Existing methods often assume single-campaign observations or rely on local heuristics, limiting robustness to severe interleaving, repeated techniques, abstraction noise, and unknown mixture cardinality. We propose Topic-Guided Consistency Modeling (TGCM), a consistency-inspired one-step framework for UKISD. TGCM maps an interleaved technique sequence to campaign episodes, jointly performing occurrence assignment and sequence reconstruction in one forward pass. It combines topic guidance from ATT&CK narratives with an embedding-space self-consistency objective to improve semantic coherence and retain efficient inference. events.excerpt: arXiv:2506.15253v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon unattended scenarios, security evaluation of them before deployment becomes increasingly essential and challenging. Existing evaluation methods mainly follow the paradigms of LLM-as-a-Judge or Agent-as-a-Judge. However, such judges are themselves often vulnerable to hallucination and can even be affected by perturbations. Furthermore, because capturing full environment states at every step is often prohibitively expensive in open-ended environments, existing evaluations typically rely on textual logs and the final environment state. As a result, they may miss transient violations that are overwritten before the trajectory ends or never reflected in textual logs. We present RAS-Eval, a specification-based security evaluation framework for LLM agents. RAS-Eval uniformly expresses utility and security objectives as Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications over tool-call trajectories and dynamic environment observations, and verifies them with an off-the-shelf model checker. This design addresses both limitations above. First, unlike LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge, RAS-Eval derives deterministic verdicts from formally defined properties, eliminating evaluator-side uncertainty and remaining reliable even for long-horizon trajectories. Second, RAS-Eval observes exactly the states on which the verdict depends, making it affordable to monitor the environment throughout execution and detect transient violations that leave little trace in the logs
events.title: Specification-based Security Evaluation of Real-World Agents Tool-Calling under Long-Horizon Context Tasks

Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. events.excerpt: Posting a factual decode of recent ACLManager role activity on Aave V3 Ethereum, in the dated-report style already used in this category. Three RISK_ADMIN_ROLE grants since 2 September 2026: 2 Sep 2026, block 25891729 — granted to 0xbe28…7744 and 0x529e…F6c5 (two grants, same transaction) 30 Sep 2026, block 26089561 — granted to 0x6f48d9cdb8ee6e17c96b2d8aec128af426a295c1 The 30 Sep recipient is a verified contract named RiskSteward, 20,061 bytes of deployed code. All three grants were sent by 0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, which is the governance Executor. So these passed governance rather than originating from a standalone admin key — worth stating explicitly, since a RISK_ADMIN grant from an EOA would read very differently. Practical scope: RISK_ADMIN can change supply and borrow caps, LTVs, liquidation thresholds and reserve configuration without a full governance vote. Routing it through a RiskSteward contract constrains what the holder may change, which is the safer pattern, but each grant still widens the set of actors who can move risk parameters between votes. Context: the ARFC “Activate Aave Risk Stewards on Aave V4” thread is now closed with AIP #523 executed, so I’m posting this separately rather than reverting that thread. Method note: this is decoded from ACLManager’s RoleGranted logs plus the role constants read off the contract itself. I have not diffed storage layouts or reviewed the RiskSteward contract’s internal constraints — so I’m not making any claim about what that specific steward is or isn’t able to do. events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Its central observation, that the protocol commits only to a circuit’s input and output and never to the layers in between, made GKR look like the natural tool for proving hash-heavy computation. A year later, that has led to what is, as far as we know, the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. This post follows that work, StateSync-GKR, from the protocol and its field to the update a circuit encodes, the Rust code and the prover arithmetic. Two arXiv papers give the details: Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates, with a Machine-Checked Core and StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine , whose appendix plots the measurements in 363 panels. All formal results are proved in the first paper, and Isabelle/HOL also checks the parts marked as machine-checked. events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. We show that a MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 300k is viable with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation while the node processes a block. At 100 tx/s (30M gas/s), block processing then stays within 50 ms, even on p90 mainnet blocks. The cost moves to the mempool, which admits only 12–27% of honest frame transactions under the flood. 1. events.excerpt: Overview Important This is the op-deployer release for op-contracts/v9.0.0+allowlist . It deploys op-contracts/v9.0.0+allowlist through the allowlist OPCM when an intent names it. It is otherwise identical to op-deployer/v0.9.0 . Other changes Deploy To deploy or upgrade a chain with op-contracts/v9.0.0+allowlist, set opcmAddress in the intent to the allowlist OPCM. That address is 0x12f00d96414fe43cc3a19acc1254d7bd83d5bed0 on Mainnet and 0xb72366fb8f855779f01800aed1ebfae886f37ace on Sepolia. This requires intent type custom or standard-overrides , because a standard intent rejects any OPCM other than the registry's. Without opcmAddress , op-deployer uses the op-contracts/v9.0.0 OPCM from the superchain registry, as v0.9.0 does ( #23929 , #23933 ) Full Changelog : op-deployer/v0.9.0...op-deployer/v0.9.0-allowlist 🚢 Docker Image: https://us-docker.pkg.dev/oplabs-tools-artifacts/images/op-deployer:v0.9.0-allowlist

events.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.
